harmonicFunction: G (I) - Tonic major chord, providing the warm foundation and resolution points

D (V) - Dominant chord creating gentle tension and forward movement
Em (vi) - Relative minor adding the emotional depth and bittersweet quality to the chorus

techniques.name: Open Chord Acoustic Strumming
techniques.description: Simple open chord strumming pattern that forms the backbone of this power ballad, using the beginner-friendly G, Cadd9, and D voicings with a gentle, rhythmic strum

notes: G: 3-2-0-0-3-3 (open G with the B note on the high E string)
Cadd9: X-3-2-0-3-0 (beautiful open voicing with 3rd fret on both B and A strings)
D: X-X-0-2-3-2 (standard open D chord)
Em: 0-2-2-0-0-0 (simple open Em, easiest chord to play)
The strumming pattern is a slow, steady down-down-up-up-down-up at 72 BPM
Let all open strings ring as much as possible for a full, warm sound
sequence: Position fingers for the G chord and strum the full pattern
Transition to Cadd9 - only the index and middle fingers move
The common 3rd-fret B-string note is shared between G and Cadd9
Move to D chord for the resolution points
Add Em when the chorus arrives for the emotional shift
tips: The G-to-Cadd9 change is one of the easiest in guitar - only two fingers move
Keep your ring finger anchored on the 3rd fret of the B string during the G-Cadd9 change
Strum lightly and evenly - this is a ballad, not a rocker
Focus on making each chord ring clean before worrying about the strumming pattern

techniques.name: Basic Fingerpicking Pattern
techniques.description: Simple fingerpicking used in the intro and quieter verse moments, plucking individual strings to outline chord shapes with a gentle, intimate feel

notes: Thumb covers the bass strings (6th, 5th, 4th strings)
Index finger covers the 3rd string
Middle finger covers the 2nd string
Ring finger covers the 1st string
The pattern alternates bass note (thumb) with treble notes (fingers)
sequence: Play the bass note with the thumb on beat 1
Follow with index, middle, ring fingers on beats 2, 3, 4
Alternate the bass note between root and fifth of each chord
Maintain the pattern through each chord change
tips: Start with just the thumb playing bass notes to establish the rhythm
Add one finger at a time until the full pattern is comfortable
The fingerpicking is optional - strumming works fine for the entire song
Keep nails short on the picking hand or use fingerpicks for clarity

techniques.name: Clean Electric Lead with Simple Bends
techniques.description: The guitar solo uses a clean or lightly overdriven electric tone with melodic phrases, simple half-step and whole-step bends, and warm sustain for an emotionally expressive lead

notes: Solo primarily uses G major pentatonic at the 7th position
Half-step bends on the B string (7th fret, bending D to D#/Eb)
Whole-step bends on the B string (8th fret, bending E to F#)
Clean or lightly overdriven tone - no heavy distortion
Vibrato applied to sustained notes for warmth
sequence: Begin with a simple melodic phrase around the 7th position
Execute a half-step bend for gentle emotional expression
Move to a whole-step bend for the climactic moment
Apply vibrato to the sustained bent note
Resolve the phrase by returning to the root (G) note
tips: Use the neck pickup for a warmer, rounder lead tone
Bends should be slow and deliberate - this is not a flashy solo
Focus on the emotional quality of each note rather than speed
CC DeVille's original solo is melodic and singable - aim for that vocal quality
details.progression: Solo over G - Cadd9 - D - G progression

sections.name: Acoustic Intro
sections.description: Gentle fingerpicked acoustic intro with G and Cadd9 chords establishing the reflective, intimate mood of the ballad
notes: Start with a soft fingerpicked pattern on the G chord
Let the open strings ring naturally for warmth
The intro sets the emotional tone - play gently and evenly
A simple strum pattern works as a beginner alternative to fingerpicking

sections.name: Verse
sections.description: The storytelling verse using the G-Cadd9 shuttle with gentle acoustic strumming, building slowly toward the D chord arrival
sections.progression: G - Cadd9 - G - Cadd9 - G - Cadd9 - D - Cadd9
notes: Keep the strumming gentle and supportive beneath the vocal melody
The D chord arrives late in the verse for a sense of gradual harmonic movement
Focus on clean chord transitions - buzzing notes are very audible in a ballad
The tempo is slow at 72 BPM - let each chord breathe

sections.name: Chorus
sections.description: The emotional chorus with the Em chord adding bittersweet depth to the 'every rose has its thorn' hook, the song's most memorable moment
sections.progression: G - Cadd9 - D - Em - Cadd9 - G - D
notes: The Em chord is the emotional heart of the chorus - accent it slightly
Strum a bit more forcefully than the verse for natural dynamics
The I-IV-V-vi progression is one of the most common in popular music
Practice the Em entrance to make it feel natural and smooth

sections.name: Verse 2
sections.description: Second verse continuing the intimate acoustic strumming, with slightly more confidence in the delivery as the song's story deepens
sections.progression: G - Cadd9 - G - Cadd9 - G - Cadd9 - D - Cadd9
notes: Slightly more dynamic than the first verse for natural song progression
Can add subtle electric guitar in the background if performing with a band
Maintain the same strumming pattern for consistency
The slow tempo allows for expressive rhythmic variations

sections.name: Chorus 2
sections.description: Second chorus with increased emotional weight and slightly stronger dynamics, preparing for the bridge and solo sections
sections.progression: G - Cadd9 - D - Em - Cadd9 - G - D
notes: Build slightly on the first chorus dynamics
The band may add electric guitar underneath for building momentum
The singalong potential peaks here - play with confidence and warmth
Prepare for the emotional shift into the bridge

sections.name: Bridge
sections.description: The bridge section starting on the Em chord for a darker emotional center, building through the chord progression toward the guitar solo climax
sections.progression: Em - D - Cadd9 - G - Em - D - Cadd9 - D
notes: Starting on Em gives the bridge a contrasting emotional quality
The descending Em-D-Cadd9 motion creates a sense of emotional release
Build intensity gradually through the bridge toward the solo
The final D chord hangs with tension before the solo entrance

sections.name: Guitar Solo
sections.technique: Clean Electric Lead with Simple Bends
sections.description: CC DeVille's melodic guitar solo with clean electric tone, simple bends, and warm phrasing over the verse chord progression
notes: Clean or lightly overdriven tone - the solo should sound warm, not aggressive
G major pentatonic at the 7th position is the primary scale home
Simple half-step and whole-step bends for emotional expression
The solo is melodic and singable - focus on phrasing over speed

sections.name: Final Chorus
sections.description: The final chorus with maximum emotional weight, building to the song's conclusion with repeated hook and gentle resolution
sections.progression: G - Cadd9 - D - Em - Cadd9 - G - D - G
notes: Peak emotional intensity for the final chorus delivery
The final G chord should ring out and sustain to close the song
Can add gentle harmonics on the final chord for a beautiful ending
The crowd singalong peaks here - play with warmth and conviction

alternatives: Fender Stratocaster for the electric solo sections
guitar.pickup: Acoustic piezo for amplified performance; neck single-coil for the clean electric solo

amp.recommended: Fender Twin Reverb (clean channel for electric solo)
alternatives: Any acoustic amplifier for the acoustic sections

settings.gain: 2-3 (clean to very light breakup for the solo)

effects.distortion: None for acoustic sections. Very light overdrive (barely breaking up) for the electric solo.
effects.delay: Light analog delay (300-400ms) with one or two repeats for the solo
effects.reverb: Medium spring or hall reverb for warmth and depth on both acoustic and electric tones
effects.other: Chorus pedal optional for thickening the clean electric tone. No heavy effects needed - simplicity is key.

beginner.focus: Master the three open chord shapes and basic strumming pattern - this is an ideal first song
steps: Learn the G, Cadd9, and D open chord shapes individually
Practice switching between G and Cadd9 (the easiest two-chord change in guitar)
Add the D chord and practice the full G-Cadd9-D progression
Learn a simple down-strum pattern at 72 BPM and play along with the recording
beginner.timeEstimate: 1-2 weeks for verse and chorus strumming

intermediate.focus: Add the Em chord, fingerpicking pattern, and dynamic nuance between sections
steps: Add Em to the chord vocabulary for the chorus and bridge
Learn the basic fingerpicking pattern for the intro
Work on dynamic contrast between gentle verses and more forceful choruses
Practice the complete song structure from intro to final chorus
intermediate.timeEstimate: 2-3 weeks for the full acoustic arrangement

advanced.focus: Learn the electric guitar solo, add expressive techniques, and refine performance dynamics
steps: Learn the G major pentatonic scale at the 7th position
Practice half-step and whole-step bends with accurate pitch
Work through the solo melody phrase by phrase
Refine the complete song with both acoustic rhythm and electric solo
advanced.timeEstimate: 3-4 weeks for complete performance with solo

commonMistakes: Strumming too hard - this is a gentle ballad, not a power chord workout
Buzzing strings on chord changes due to incomplete finger placement
Rushing the slow 72 BPM tempo - patience is essential for ballads
Neglecting the Em chord in the chorus, which is the emotional core of the song
practiceRoutine: Warm up with G-Cadd9 chord transitions for 3 minutes (the easiest change in the song)
Practice the verse strumming pattern with G-Cadd9-D at 72 BPM (5 minutes)
Work on the chorus adding the Em chord transition (5 minutes)
Practice the fingerpicking intro pattern slowly (5 minutes)
Full song run-through with acoustic guitar (5 minutes)
focusAreas: Clean open chord voicings without any buzzing strings
Smooth chord transitions especially to and from the D chord
Gentle, even strumming at the slow 72 BPM ballad tempo
Dynamic control between quiet verses and more emotional choruses
metronomeWork: Practice chord changes with metronome at 72 BPM from the start (tempo is already slow)
Count along with the metronome: 1-2-3-4 for each bar, one chord per bar
Practice the fingerpicking pattern with metronome eighth notes at 72 BPM
Build confidence by playing through the full progression without pausing between chords
